verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section praising learning: the three kinds of people.
verse.sanskrit: प्रारभ्यते न खलु विघ्नभयेन नीचैः प्रारभ्य विघ्नविहता विरमन्ति मध्याः ॥ विघ्नैः पुनः पुनरपि प्रतिहन्यमानाः प्रारब्धमुत्तमगुणा न परित्यजन्ति ॥
verse.line: Some never start for fear of obstacles; some quit when obstacles hit. The best keep going.
verse.translation: The lowest do not begin at all, for fear of obstacles. The middling begin, but stop when obstacles strike. The best, struck by obstacles again and again, do not give up what they have begun.
verse.why: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.
verse.misuse: Perseverance is not refusing ever to change course; weigh honestly whether the goal still deserves you.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: In praise of learning and the learned
prasang.summary: Bhartrihari praises learning as wealth no thief can take and speech as the one lasting ornament, then turns to good company and the three kinds of people who face obstacles. It ends with the 'sword's-edge vow' of the good.
prasang.lesson: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to you from his text on the value of learning, describing the three kinds of people who meet obstacles. The lowest never begin, fearing what might go wrong. The middling start, but stop when trouble arrives. The best, struck by obstacles again and again, do not give up what they have begun. The point is that what you learn and how you speak are wealth no one can take from you. The truth underneath is that starting and staying are different, and the real failure is not the obstacle but the stopping.
verse.for_you: You have been going for years with this side project, and you no longer know if you are stuck in discipline or in stubbornness. You do not need to know the whole path today.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son Sanjaya, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: सर्वेषां कर्मणां तात फले नित्यमनित्यता / अनित्यमिति जानन्तो न भवन्ति भवन्ति च अथ ये नैव कुर्वन्ति नैव जातु भवन्ति ते / ऐकगुण्यमनीहायामभावः कर्मणां फलम्
verse.line: Every result is uncertain. Some who try succeed and some don't. Those who never try never do.
verse.translation: The result of every action is uncertain. Knowing this, some people act and succeed, some do not. But those who never act never succeed at all.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.for_you: No effort on the right path is ever wasted; even a little of it protects you and carries you forward.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Draupadi
verse.setting: Draupadi argues that waiting on fate is no plan: people must act.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वतो नार्थसिद्धिर्मे भवतीति ह भारत / निर्वेदो नात्र गन्तव्यो द्वावन्तौ यस्य कर्मणः
verse.line: Don't despair because effort hasn't paid off yet. Every attempt can go either way.
verse.translation: 'I keep working and still don't succeed' is no reason to despair. Every effort can end two ways, in success or not; only by not acting is the outcome certain.
verse.why: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

prasang.title: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

verse.for_you: The self is never stuck; it is the mind that hesitates, while what you truly are is already free and able.

verse.speaker: Tulsidas
verse.setting: Tulsidas, after trying and failing to set himself right.
verse.sanskrit: मेरी न बने बनाये मेरे कोटि कलप लौं राम! रावरे बनाये बने पल पाउ मैं।
verse.line: What I could not fix in ages, grace can mend in a moment.
verse.translation: What I try to make of myself would not come right in millions of ages; Ram, what you make comes right in a quarter of a moment.
verse.misuse: Not a reason to stop trying; a release from the belief that everything rests on you.
verse.meaning: Tulsidas, after years of trying and failing to set himself right, speaks to Ram. He says that what he could not fix in millions of ages, grace can mend in a quarter of a moment. He offers that the part of you that keeps trying is enough, and the result does not rest entirely on your shoulders. The verse proposes that you do not have to carry the weight of every failed attempt alone.
verse.for_you: The part of you that keeps trying to build these apps is enough, even when the result stays hidden. Your worth is not measured by what has come back to you yet.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna, who asks why he must act at all if understanding is higher.
verse.sanskrit: नियतं कुरु कर्म त्वं कर्म ज्यायो ह्यकर्मणः । शरीरयात्रापि च ते न प्रसिद्ध्येदकर्मणः ॥
verse.line: Do the work that's yours. Doing something beats doing nothing; even living needs action.
verse.translation: Do your allotted work, for action is better than inaction. Even the maintenance of your body would not be possible without action.
verse.why: Not acting is still a choice; do the work that is yours.

prasang.title: Why doing your duty without attachment is better
prasang.summary: Arjuna is confused and asks for one clear answer. Krishna says no one can stop acting, that repressing the body while the mind indulges is self-deception, and that action beats inaction.
prasang.lesson: Not acting is still a choice; do the work that is yours.

verse.meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna, who asks why he must act if understanding is higher. Krishna says do your allotted work, for action is better than inaction. Even the maintenance of your body would not be possible without action. He explains that not acting is still a choice, and doing something beats doing nothing.
verse.for_you: Pick one small thing that belongs to you alone and do it today. Do not wait for the outcome to tell you it was the right step. Just act, because doing something beats doing nothing.

verse.speaker: Medhavin
verse.setting: A young man named Medhavin urges his father not to keep postponing what truly matters.
verse.sanskrit: श्वः कार्यमद्य कुर्वीत पूर्वाह्णे चापराह्णिकम् / नहि प्रतीक्षते मृत्युः कृतमस्य न वा कृतम्
verse.line: Do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's in the morning. Time doesn't wait for you to be ready.
verse.translation: Do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's work in the morning. Death does not wait to see whether your work is done or not.
verse.why: Life slips away while we stay busy. Do what matters now.
verse.misuse: About not postponing what matters, not about working nonstop.

prasang.title: Medhavin: the son who woke his father
prasang.summary: A father lays out the conventional path of study, family and ritual. His son Medhavin replies that days and nights fall like arrows and death takes people mid-task, so do tomorrow's work today and live truthfully now.
prasang.lesson: Life slips away while we stay busy. Do what matters now.

verse.meaning: A young man named Medhavin speaks to his father, who is lying in bed, laying out the usual path of study, family, and ritual. Medhavin says the days and nights fall like arrows and death can take a person mid-task. He urges his father to do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's in the morning. Life slips away while we wait to be ready. The verse proposes that waiting for the perfect moment is a trap, and that doing what is yours now is the only way to live truthfully.
verse.for_you: You have been waiting for a sign that your project is working, but that sign may never come. Today, do one small thing that belongs only to you. Send one email, sketch one screen, or write one line of code. Do it without waiting for the result to tell you it was right.

story.title: Hanuman's leap
story.story_hook: Halfway across the ocean, a golden mountain rose out of the water and offered him a place to rest.
story.summary: Hanuman leaps across the ocean. A mountain rises to repay an old kindness by offering rest; he thanks it but keeps his promise not to stop. He outwits Surasa by shrinking small and defeats Simhika, and the watching beings praise his steadiness, sight, judgement and skill.
story.lesson: Gratitude and focus can go together; know when to be big and when to be small.

script: You have been running on all these tracks, the full-time work, the children, the parents, and this app you have built for years. The failure has worn you down until you cannot tell if you are being disciplined or just stubborn. You feel like you have stopped knowing what is wrong.

Bhartrihari wrote this to the reader from his text on the value of learning. He was looking at the three kinds of people when trouble arrives. The lowest never begin, fearing what might go wrong. Bhartrihari said:
प्रारभ्यते न खलु विघ्नभयेन नीचैः प्रारभ्य विघ्नविहता विरमन्ति मध्याः. विघ्नैः पुनः पुनरपि प्रतिहन्यमानाः प्रारब्धमुत्तमगुणा न परित्यजन्ति.
In plain words: Some never start for fear of obstacles; some quit when obstacles hit. The best keep going.

What he is pointing to is a difference between starting and staying. The real failure is not the obstacle but the stopping, because the lowest and the middling both end up not finishing what they began. This is easier said than done, because when you have carried a project for years without a clear result, your mind learns to wait for a sign before it will move again.

You do not need to know if this is discipline or stubbornness right now. You do not need to see the whole path. You only need to name the one thing you can do today, without waiting for the result to tell you it was right.
What is the one step you can take today without waiting for a sign?

depth.life: You are holding a full-time job, children, and aging parents, and you are still trying to build your app on the side. You have been at this for years without a clear result, and now you feel tired of failing and of not knowing what is wrong.
depth.points: The texts point to a mind that has learned to wait for a sign before it will start again, mistaking caution for wisdom and turning your own effort into a source of doubt.
depth.practice: Write down the one small step your app needs today, and take it without checking if it is the right step.
depth.question: What would it look like to do one thing today without waiting for the result to tell you it was right?
